paras: The lynching of Ben Theophil was the hanging of an Italian railroad laborer, also named in reports as Pete Theophil or Ben Peters, by masked men at Gunnison, Colorado, about midnight on Friday, October 28, 1881. Accused of shooting railroad contractor W. L. Hoblitzell, he was taken from a guarded room in the Gunnison court house on the night of his capture and hanged from a livery stable sign. Wire dispatches reported it nationally as a hanging 'by the citizens,' while the Elk Mountain Pilot questioned the lynching and the guarding of the prisoner.

Hoblitzell, spelled 'Hobletzel' in the wires, was a Cumberland, Maryland, contractor building part of the Denver and Rio Grande line in the Black Canyon west of Gunnison. A Denver dispatch said that days earlier, during a row between Irish and Italian laborers, an attempt had been made to hang the same Italian and Hoblitzell had rescued him. According to a camp letter of October 27 by T. F. McCardell, the laborer demanded his pay that morning, was refused under a ten-day notice rule, struggled with Hoblitzell when told to leave, and then shot him from the doorway. Hoblitzell died that night.

Sheriff George Yule left the camp that evening with two workmen, Peter Smith and A. S. Albright, and at dawn the three captured the fugitive beside a roadside camp fire. Returning, they ran past a crowd of angry men at the Hoblitzell camp who shouted for the prisoner, and reached Gunnison shortly after 4 p.m. on Friday. Fearing an outbreak, officers moved him from the jail to the court house.

At midnight masked men entered the court room; the New Bloomfield Times said two of them held Under-Sheriff Clark while others took the Italian from a bench where he was sleeping. They put a rope around his neck, dragged him down the stairs and through the snow to a livery stable on Tumichi avenue, and hanged him from its sign. He was probably dead before the stable was reached, the New Bloomfield Times judged, and the body was found hanging on Saturday morning.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage. The Elk Mountain Pilot contrasted the case with 1880, when a prisoner named Breckinridge had been heavily guarded in the Gunnison jail against citizens who meant to hang him.

Before the lynching, the shooting ran under headlines such as 'An Italian Assassin' in the Salt Lake Herald and 'A Treacherous Italian' in the Washington Evening Star. A Gunnison dispatch of October 29 then reported in two sentences that 'his murderer' had been taken from jail and hanged 'by the citizens.' The Chicago Tribune headed it 'A Murderer Lynched' and the Cheyenne Daily Leader 'Western Justice,' and it also ran in the Helena Weekly Herald and the Rocky Mountain Husbandman. Weeklies such as the Mower County Transcript, the Crawford Avalanche and the Superior Times reduced it to one sentence; none named the dead man.

The Elk Mountain Pilot was the one paper to object, writing that although 'the victim may have got his just deserts,' taking a man 'from the court house during a term of court' looked 'a little bad.' The fullest accounts appeared weeks later in Pennsylvania and Maryland papers near Hoblitzell's former home. The New Bloomfield Times told the manhunt as reading 'with all the interest of a western novel,' but called the lynchers a 'murderous gang' and the hanging body 'a splendid monument of Gunnison's efficient city government.'

The accused's name was given as Ben or Pete Theophil in the camp letter and as Ben Peters by the Colorado Springs Gazette. The wires said he was taken from the jail, but the later, more detailed accounts place the seizure in the court house and are the better evidence. The Somerset Herald described a 'strong guard' covered by masked men, while the Elk Mountain Pilot said Clark guarded him alone and opened the door to the mob's knock, saying he had sent for more guards. Denver Republican specials described a pursuit by the sheriff and about a hundred laborers, while the New Bloomfield Times said he chose two men from the hundred who volunteered.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Hobletzel died and shortly afterward his murderer was taken from jail and hanged by the citizens.

accounts.label: Cumberland Daily News / Denver Republican specials
accounts.gist: After a pay dispute and struggle, Theophil shot Hoblitzell; captured with a $1,000 reward out, he was moved to the court house under strong guard, where masked men covered the guards, took him and hanged him to a livery stable sign.

accounts.label: Elk Mountain Pilot
accounts.gist: Under-Sheriff Clark guarded the prisoner alone in the court room and opened the door at midnight to an armed mob; Clark said he had sent for more guards.

accounts.label: New Bloomfield Times narrative
accounts.gist: Sheriff Yule and two workmen captured 'Pete' at dawn and ran past an angry crowd at the camp; at Gunnison masked men held Clark, seized the sleeping prisoner and dragged him by the neck to the livery sign, probably dead on arrival.

accounts.label: Colorado Springs Gazette
accounts.gist: Ben Peters, beaten in a fight with Hoblitzell, returned with a pistol and shot him, and was hung to the sign on a livery stable.

framing.detail: The Oct. 29 wire ran as 'A Murderer Lynched' (Chicago Tribune) and 'Western Justice' (Cheyenne), calling the dead man 'his murderer' and the lynchers 'the citizens.'
Pre-lynching headlines 'A Treacherous Italian' and 'An Italian Assassin' identified the accused only by nationality.
The Elk Mountain Pilot did not approve, though 'the victim may have got his just deserts,' and faulted the guarding.
The New Bloomfield Times called the lynchers a 'murderous gang' and the hanging body 'a splendid monument of Gunnison's efficient city government,' while praising the capture as a 'thrilling' story.
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer's obituary of Hoblitzell noted without comment that the Italian was 'promptly lynched.'
